title: A Saturday at the Repair Table
mainTextWithPlaceholders: Our neighbourhood repair table began with three folding chairs and a box of borrowed tools. Visitors bring lamps, radios, and small household objects that have {{1}} working. The volunteers do not simply fix each item; they invite its owner to inspect the problem with them. This approach takes longer, but it gives people the confidence to attempt simple repairs {{2}} their own. Last month, the group saved forty-two objects from being thrown away. It also collected short notes about the most common faults, {{3}} future workshops could focus on useful skills. The organisers are careful not to promise that every object can be rescued. Even so, owners often leave satisfied because they understand {{4}} went wrong and what to check next time.
learningObjectives: Select verbs and connectors from grammatical and collocational context
Use local cohesion to distinguish plausible distractors

options.feedback: ‘Stopped working’ is the natural verb pattern for a device that no longer functions.

options.text: closed
options.feedback: ‘Closed’ does not combine with ‘working’ in this meaning.

options.text: paused
options.feedback: A device can pause, but ‘paused working’ is not the intended construction.

options.text: ended
options.feedback: ‘Ended working’ is not idiomatic here.

options.text: by
options.feedback: ‘By their own’ is incomplete; it would require a different phrase.

options.text: on
options.feedback: ‘On their own’ means independently.

options.text: from
options.feedback: ‘From their own’ does not form the fixed expression.

options.text: with
options.feedback: ‘With their own’ would need a following noun.

options.text: unless
options.feedback: The sentence expresses a result or purpose, not an exception.

options.text: whereas
options.feedback: No contrast is being drawn between two facts.

options.text: so
options.feedback: ‘So’ connects the collected evidence to its intended practical use.

options.text: although
options.feedback: The second clause does not concede or contradict the first.

options.text: that
options.feedback: ‘That’ cannot ask about the cause in this embedded clause.

options.feedback: There is no defined set of alternatives for ‘which’ to select from.

options.text: how
options.feedback: ‘How went wrong’ is not grammatical.

options.text: what
options.feedback: ‘What went wrong’ is the correct embedded question.

title: The Seed Shelf
mainTextWithPlaceholders: A small shelf appeared beside the entrance to Brook Lane Library in March. It was full {{1}} packets of vegetable and flower seeds. Anyone could take a packet, provided that they promised to return some seeds after the plants had grown. At first, the librarians were not sure {{2}} the idea would work. Within two weeks, however, every packet had found a home. Local gardeners then began adding labels with simple advice, such as how much sunlight each plant needed. The shelf has become more {{3}} a place to exchange seeds: people now leave notes offering spare pots or help to new gardeners. There is no membership form, {{4}} participants are asked to take only what they can use.
learningObjectives: Complete common fixed phrases with function words
Use clause meaning to choose a conjunction

questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is ‘full of’.
An indirect yes-or-no question can use ‘whether’ or ‘if’.
The expression ‘more than’ shows that the shelf now has an additional social role.
‘But’ contrasts the absence of a form with the presence of a request.

title: Mapping a City After Dark
mainTextWithPlaceholders: A university team asked residents to record how they moved through the city after dark. The researchers were interested not only in {{1}}, but also in whether public spaces felt welcoming. Participants used a simple map to mark bright routes, quiet corners, and places where signs were {{2}}. The project produced several {{3}} findings. For example, a well-lit path was not always the preferred route if it felt isolated. City planners have since added evening walks to their consultation process, giving residents a more {{4}} role in decisions about lighting and transport.
learningObjectives: Use suffixes and prefixes while preserving meaning

questions.questionText: EXPECT
questions.explanation: An adjective meaning ‘not anticipated’ modifies ‘findings’.

questions.explanation: An adjective is needed before ‘role’.

title: Listening to the Town
mainTextWithPlaceholders: When Mara joined a guided sound walk, she expected the leader to explain local history. Instead, the group stood silently beside a fountain and wrote down every sound they noticed. At first, Mara recorded only obvious noises: buses, footsteps, and birds. After several minutes, she began to separate the splash of the fountain from the soft mechanical hum beneath it. The group then walked through a covered market, where their notes became surprisingly different. One participant focused on voices, while another noticed the rhythm of shutters being raised. The leader explained that a sound walk does not require special equipment or expert hearing. Its purpose is to make familiar places feel less automatic. Mara later repeated the activity on her usual route to work. She did not discover a hidden musical masterpiece, but she did notice which streets made her hurry and which ones helped her think. She now takes a quieter route twice a week, even though it adds five minutes to the journey.
learningObjectives: Identify purpose, detail, and implied attitude in an original text
Distinguish a supported inference from an attractive but unsupported claim

title: The Tool Library That Learnt to Say No
mainTextWithPlaceholders:
The River Quarter Tool Library opened with a simple promise: residents could borrow equipment that was expensive to buy but rarely used. Membership grew quickly, and the shelves filled with drills, ladders, sewing machines, and gardening tools. {{1}} The success created an unexpected problem, however. Volunteers were spending so much time checking equipment that they could no longer help members learn how to use it.

The committee first considered limiting membership. {{2}} Instead, it studied which loans created the most work. The data showed that a small number of complicated machines accounted for most late returns and safety checks. The library stopped accepting those machines and published a clear explanation.

Some members complained that the decision made the collection less impressive. {{3}} Within a month, waiting times fell and volunteers restarted their Saturday workshops. Attendance at those sessions soon exceeded the number of people who had borrowed the removed machines.

The experience changed how the committee measured success. It still records membership and loans, but it now tracks whether people gain confidence with a skill. {{4}} By narrowing the collection, the library became better at fulfilling its real purpose: helping neighbours make and repair things together.
learningObjectives: Trace argument structure and reference across paragraphs
Select missing sentences by function, not keyword overlap

options.text: That would have reduced demand, but it would not have addressed what was consuming the volunteers' time.
A short conversation after each workshop provides richer evidence for that question than a loan total ever could.
At first, the team regarded every new loan as proof that the model was working.
Other organisations responded by offering to store the entire collection in distant warehouses.
Yet the change also made the service more reliable for the items that remained.

title: Four Views on Public Rooftop Gardens
mainTextWithPlaceholders: Four writers consider whether public buildings should host rooftop gardens. Match each question to the writer whose position it describes most accurately.
learningObjectives: Compare nuanced positions across short argumentative texts
Identify qualified agreement, reservation, and underlying assumptions

questions.questionText: Who argues that symbolic value can justify a project even when direct output is modest?
Who is most concerned that enthusiasm may conceal continuing operational costs?
Who sees the proposal primarily as a way to build practical knowledge?
Who thinks the physical site should be selected only after consulting likely participants?

texts.title: A Classroom Above the Street
texts.content: The harvest will never feed an entire district, and that should not be the test. A rooftop plot lets residents compare soil mixtures, observe insects, and understand why watering systems fail. If the project is designed around workshops rather than impressive photographs, its educational return could be substantial. The budget should therefore include trained facilitators, not just beds and plants.

texts.title: Budget for Year Five
texts.content: Opening-day volunteers are easy to find; people willing to inspect drainage in winter are not. Proposals routinely celebrate donated timber and free seedlings while treating maintenance as if it disappears after launch. Any public body considering a garden should publish a five-year staffing and repair budget first. Without that, a neglected rooftop may become an expensive lesson in wishful thinking.

texts.title: Start with the People
texts.content: Planners often begin by identifying the flattest roof and then search for users. The order should be reversed. A site near a senior centre might need shade and seating, while one above a youth workshop could support experiments and noisy group activity. Ask participants what they would sustain, then find a building that suits the resulting programme. Architecture is a constraint, not the mission.

texts.title: A Visible Commitment
texts.content: Critics correctly note that rooftop crops are costly compared with produce from ordinary farms. Yet public projects also communicate priorities. A carefully maintained garden above a library can make heat, rainwater, and urban biodiversity visible to thousands of visitors. Its output should still be measured honestly, but a modest harvest does not make the project empty if it changes what a community is willing to discuss.
